title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:
The invitations were ready, but the rooftops were not a simple road. Ada counted 3 papers, Pip warmed his cheeks for a helpful puff, and Mara checked the nearby pots. “No daring guesses,” Mara said. Ada nodded. “We will notice, test, and change our method if we need to.” Above them, the marker ribbon began to dance.

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a gentle breeze. “It is only strength 1,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Pip gave the ribbon a tiny warm puff. It lifted neatly and settled without whipping away. His eyes widened. “I can make a small breeze,” he said. Ada grinned. “Small and steady is exactly what we need.”

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 1 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

Ada peered along the roofline toward the glasshouse. The route was open, with no fallen tools or blocked stepping stones. She pointed it out to Mara. “That path may be useful,” she said, “if the wind agrees.”

The calm route was open, so Ada and Mara carried the dry invitations by hand. They walked slowly past the planters and placed each paper with the labeled pots. “No flight needed,” Mara said. “Good noticing did the traveling.” The labeled pots now held the complete invitation bundle, a bright row of proof that their careful arrangement had worked.

title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:

Ada nodded. “We will notice, test, and change our method if we need to.” Above them, the marker ribbon began to dance.

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a brisk breeze. “It is only strength 2,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 2 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

Mara placed the ready pouch in Ada’s hands. “Keep it low and tied,” she said. Ada accepted it carefully. The pouch was no longer merely waiting at the post; it was now part of their working arrangement.

Pip gave the ribbon a tiny warm puff. It lifted neatly and settled without whipping away. His eyes widened. “I can make a small breeze,” he said. Ada grinned. “Small and steady is exactly what we need.”

Mara passed Ada the coil of twine. “A line gives the pouch a boundary,” she explained. Ada tested the cord between her fingers. “So Pip can guide the bundle without chasing it,” she replied.

Ada peered along the roofline toward the glasshouse. The route was open, with no fallen tools or blocked stepping stones. She pointed it out to Mara. “That path may be useful,” she said, “if the wind agrees.”

Ada and Mara stretched the twine between safe roof posts and tied firm knots. Mara pulled the line once; it answered with a quiet twang. “That is a road with rails,” Ada said.

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Ada placed the invitations in the pouch while Pip held its mouth open with careful claws. Together they tied it shut. The papers were secured inside, not merely imagined there. Pip whispered, “No heroic gusts.” Ada replied, “Only tested ones.”

With the pouch tied to the guiding line, Ada watched the stopping point while Pip gave measured warm puffs. The pouch slid, paused, and slid again instead of flying. At the glasshouse, the invitations reached the labeled pots together. The labeled pots now held the complete invitation bundle, a bright row of proof that their careful arrangement had worked.

title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:
The invitations were ready, but the rooftops were not a simple road. Ada counted 4 papers, Pip warmed his cheeks for a helpful puff, and Mara checked the nearby pots. “No daring guesses,” Mara said. Ada nodded. “We will notice, test, and change our method if we need to.” Above them, the marker ribbon began to dance.

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Ada looked toward the glasshouse and found the route closed. A small gate barred the way. “That settles it,” she said. “We need the sheltered chimney nook instead of pretending a closed path is open.”

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a brisk breeze. “It is only strength 2,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Because the glasshouse route was closed, Mara lent Ada the light basket. “Cover the papers,” she warned. Ada nodded, and Pip peered over the rim. “A basket can travel on the safe side,” Ada said.

Pip tried a tiny warm puff, but the ribbon bobbed sideways and nearly brushed a pot. He stopped at once. “My breath is wobbly today,” he admitted. Ada answered, “Then we will use your eyes and ears, not a big puff.”

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 2 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

Mara passed Ada the coil of twine. “A line gives the pouch a boundary,” she explained. Ada tested the cord between her fingers. “So Pip can guide the bundle without chasing it,” she replied.

Ada and Mara stretched the twine between safe roof posts and tied firm knots. Mara pulled the line once; it answered with a quiet twang. “That is a road with rails,” Ada said.

Mara placed the ready pouch in Ada’s hands. “Keep it low and tied,” she said. Ada accepted it carefully. The pouch was no longer merely waiting at the post; it was now part of their working arrangement.

Pip’s breath was not ready for cargo, so Ada and Mara chose the sheltered route. They carried small dry batches through the chimney nook, with Pip watching the ribbon and calling, “Gust coming!” Every invitation reached its safe resting place. The complete bundle now rested in the chimney nook, safely covered in its final arrangement beneath the shelter.

title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:
Before sunset, Ada had 3 garden-party invitations waiting at the roof post. Pip the young dragon stood beside her, eager to help, while Mara watched the roof paths and the planters below. The ribbon wind-marker flickered. “We need every invitation to arrive safely,” Ada said. “Then we should find out what the roof is telling us first.”

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Pip gave the ribbon a tiny warm puff. It lifted neatly and settled without whipping away. His eyes widened. “I can make a small breeze,” he said. Ada grinned. “Small and steady is exactly what we need.”

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a gentle breeze. “It is only strength 1,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Ada looked toward the glasshouse and found the route closed. A small gate barred the way. “That settles it,” she said. “We need the sheltered chimney nook instead of pretending a closed path is open.”

Because the glasshouse route was closed, Mara lent Ada the light basket. “Cover the papers,” she warned. Ada nodded, and Pip peered over the rim. “A basket can travel on the safe side,” Ada said.

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 1 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

Ada settled the invitations into the light basket. Pip helped lower the cloth cover, and Ada tucked every corner beneath the rim. The bundle could no longer skate away in a sudden breeze.

Pip nudged the covered basket in short, gentle bursts. Ada watched its feet skim the safe route and called, “Stop!” whenever the basket neared an edge. It arrived in the chimney nook, where the invitations rested beneath shelter. The complete bundle now rested in the chimney nook, safely covered in its final arrangement beneath the shelter.

title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:
The invitations were ready, but the rooftops were not a simple road. Ada counted 4 papers, Pip warmed his cheeks for a helpful puff, and Mara checked the nearby pots. “No daring guesses,” Mara said. Ada nodded. “We will notice, test, and change our method if we need to.” Above them, the marker ribbon began to dance.

Pip gave the ribbon a tiny warm puff. It lifted neatly and settled without whipping away. His eyes widened. “I can make a small breeze,” he said. Ada grinned. “Small and steady is exactly what we need.”

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a brisk breeze. “It is only strength 2,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Ada peered along the roofline toward the glasshouse. The route was open, with no fallen tools or blocked stepping stones. She pointed it out to Mara. “That path may be useful,” she said, “if the wind agrees.”

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 2 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

Mara passed Ada the coil of twine. “A line gives the pouch a boundary,” she explained. Ada tested the cord between her fingers. “So Pip can guide the bundle without chasing it,” she replied.

Ada and Mara stretched the twine between safe roof posts and tied firm knots. Mara pulled the line once; it answered with a quiet twang. “That is a road with rails,” Ada said.

Mara placed the ready pouch in Ada’s hands. “Keep it low and tied,” she said. Ada accepted it carefully. The pouch was no longer merely waiting at the post; it was now part of their working arrangement.

Ada placed the invitations in the pouch while Pip held its mouth open with careful claws. Together they tied it shut. The papers were secured inside, not merely imagined there. Pip whispered, “No heroic gusts.” Ada replied, “Only tested ones.”

With the pouch tied to the guiding line, Ada watched the stopping point while Pip gave measured warm puffs. The pouch slid, paused, and slid again instead of flying. At the glasshouse, the invitations reached the labeled pots together. The labeled pots now held the complete invitation bundle, a bright row of proof that their careful arrangement had worked.

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a brisk breeze. “It is only strength 2,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Pip gave the ribbon a tiny warm puff. It lifted neatly and settled without whipping away. His eyes widened. “I can make a small breeze,” he said. Ada grinned. “Small and steady is exactly what we need.”

title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:
The invitations were ready, but the rooftops were not a simple road. Ada counted 4 papers, Pip warmed his cheeks for a helpful puff, and Mara checked the nearby pots. “No daring guesses,” Mara said. Ada nodded. “We will notice, test, and change our method if we need to.” Above them, the marker ribbon began to dance.

Pip tried a tiny warm puff, but the ribbon bobbed sideways and nearly brushed a pot. He stopped at once. “My breath is wobbly today,” he admitted. Ada answered, “Then we will use your eyes and ears, not a big puff.”

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a brisk breeze. “It is only strength 2,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Ada peered along the roofline toward the glasshouse. The route was open, with no fallen tools or blocked stepping stones. She pointed it out to Mara. “That path may be useful,” she said, “if the wind agrees.”

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 2 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

Mara placed the ready pouch in Ada’s hands. “Keep it low and tied,” she said. Ada accepted it carefully. The pouch was no longer merely waiting at the post; it was now part of their working arrangement.

Mara passed Ada the coil of twine. “A line gives the pouch a boundary,” she explained. Ada tested the cord between her fingers. “So Pip can guide the bundle without chasing it,” she replied.

Ada and Mara stretched the twine between safe roof posts and tied firm knots. Mara pulled the line once; it answered with a quiet twang. “That is a road with rails,” Ada said.

Pip’s breath was not ready for cargo, so Ada and Mara chose the sheltered route. They carried small dry batches through the chimney nook, with Pip watching the ribbon and calling, “Gust coming!” Every invitation reached its safe resting place. The complete bundle now rested in the chimney nook, safely covered in its final arrangement beneath the shelter.

title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:
Before sunset, Ada had 4 garden-party invitations waiting at the roof post. Pip the young dragon stood beside her, eager to help, while Mara watched the roof paths and the planters below. The ribbon wind-marker flickered. “We need every invitation to arrive safely,” Ada said. “Then we should find out what the roof is telling us first.”

Mara turned the cloth pouch inside out and found its loose seam. With twine and careful little stitches, she repaired it. She tugged the mouth twice. “Now it will hold,” she said, “but only because we checked it first.”

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a brisk breeze. “It is only strength 2,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Ada peered along the roofline toward the glasshouse. The route was open, with no fallen tools or blocked stepping stones. She pointed it out to Mara. “That path may be useful,” she said, “if the wind agrees.”

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 2 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

Mara passed Ada the coil of twine. “A line gives the pouch a boundary,” she explained. Ada tested the cord between her fingers. “So Pip can guide the bundle without chasing it,” she replied.

Mara placed the ready pouch in Ada’s hands. “Keep it low and tied,” she said. Ada accepted it carefully. The pouch was no longer merely waiting at the post; it was now part of their working arrangement.

Pip gave the ribbon a tiny warm puff. It lifted neatly and settled without whipping away. His eyes widened. “I can make a small breeze,” he said. Ada grinned. “Small and steady is exactly what we need.”

Ada and Mara stretched the twine between safe roof posts and tied firm knots. Mara pulled the line once; it answered with a quiet twang. “That is a road with rails,” Ada said.

Ada placed the invitations in the pouch while Pip held its mouth open with careful claws. Together they tied it shut. The papers were secured inside, not merely imagined there. Pip whispered, “No heroic gusts.” Ada replied, “Only tested ones.”

With the pouch tied to the guiding line, Ada watched the stopping point while Pip gave measured warm puffs. The pouch slid, paused, and slid again instead of flying. At the glasshouse, the invitations reached the labeled pots together. The labeled pots now held the complete invitation bundle, a bright row of proof that their careful arrangement had worked.

title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:
The invitations were ready, but the rooftops were not a simple road. Ada counted 3 papers, Pip warmed his cheeks for a helpful puff, and Mara checked the nearby pots. “No daring guesses,” Mara said. Ada nodded. “We will notice, test, and change our method if we need to.” Above them, the marker ribbon began to dance.

Ada peered along the roofline toward the glasshouse. The route was open, with no fallen tools or blocked stepping stones. She pointed it out to Mara. “That path may be useful,” she said, “if the wind agrees.”

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a brisk breeze. “It is only strength 2,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 2 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Pip gave the ribbon a tiny warm puff. It lifted neatly and settled without whipping away. His eyes widened. “I can make a small breeze,” he said. Ada grinned. “Small and steady is exactly what we need.”

Mara turned the cloth pouch inside out and found its loose seam. With twine and careful little stitches, she repaired it. She tugged the mouth twice. “Now it will hold,” she said, “but only because we checked it first.”

Mara placed the ready pouch in Ada’s hands. “Keep it low and tied,” she said. Ada accepted it carefully. The pouch was no longer merely waiting at the post; it was now part of their working arrangement.

Mara passed Ada the coil of twine. “A line gives the pouch a boundary,” she explained. Ada tested the cord between her fingers. “So Pip can guide the bundle without chasing it,” she replied.

Ada and Mara stretched the twine between safe roof posts and tied firm knots. Mara pulled the line once; it answered with a quiet twang. “That is a road with rails,” Ada said.

Ada placed the invitations in the pouch while Pip held its mouth open with careful claws. Together they tied it shut. The papers were secured inside, not merely imagined there. Pip whispered, “No heroic gusts.” Ada replied, “Only tested ones.”

With the pouch tied to the guiding line, Ada watched the stopping point while Pip gave measured warm puffs. The pouch slid, paused, and slid again instead of flying. At the glasshouse, the invitations reached the labeled pots together. The labeled pots now held the complete invitation bundle, a bright row of proof that their careful arrangement had worked.

The ribbon wind-marker flickered. “We need every invitation to arrive safely,” Ada said. “Then we should find out what the roof is telling us first.”

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a gentle breeze. “It is only strength 1,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Pip tried a tiny warm puff, but the ribbon bobbed sideways and nearly brushed a pot. He stopped at once. “My breath is wobbly today,” he admitted. Ada answered, “Then we will use your eyes and ears, not a big puff.”

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 1 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

Pip’s breath was not ready for cargo, so Ada and Mara chose the sheltered route. They carried small dry batches through the chimney nook, with Pip watching the ribbon and calling, “Gust coming!” Every invitation reached its safe resting place. title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:
The invitations were ready, but the rooftops were not a simple road. Ada counted 3 papers, Pip warmed his cheeks for a helpful puff, and Mara checked the nearby pots. “No daring guesses,” Mara said. Ada nodded. “We will notice, test, and change our method if we need to.” Above them, the marker ribbon began to dance.

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Pip gave the ribbon a tiny warm puff. It lifted neatly and settled without whipping away. His eyes widened. “I can make a small breeze,” he said. Ada grinned. “Small and steady is exactly what we need.”

Ada looked toward the glasshouse and found the route closed. A small gate barred the way. “That settles it,” she said. “We need the sheltered chimney nook instead of pretending a closed path is open.”

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a gentle breeze. “It is only strength 1,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 1 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

Because the glasshouse route was closed, Mara lent Ada the light basket. “Cover the papers,” she warned. Ada nodded, and Pip peered over the rim. “A basket can travel on the safe side,” Ada said.

Ada settled the invitations into the light basket. Pip helped lower the cloth cover, and Ada tucked every corner beneath the rim. The bundle could no longer skate away in a sudden breeze.

Pip nudged the covered basket in short, gentle bursts. Ada watched its feet skim the safe route and called, “Stop!” whenever the basket neared an edge. It arrived in the chimney nook, where the invitations rested beneath shelter. The complete bundle now rested in the chimney nook, safely covered in its final arrangement beneath the shelter.

title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:
Before sunset, Ada had 3 garden-party invitations waiting at the roof post. Pip the young dragon stood beside her, eager to help, while Mara watched the roof paths and the planters below. The ribbon wind-marker flickered. “We need every invitation to arrive safely,” Ada said. “Then we should find out what the roof is telling us first.”

Pip gave the ribbon a tiny warm puff. It lifted neatly and settled without whipping away. His eyes widened. “I can make a small breeze,” he said. Ada grinned. “Small and steady is exactly what we need.”

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Ada peered along the roofline toward the glasshouse. The route was open, with no fallen tools or blocked stepping stones. She pointed it out to Mara. “That path may be useful,” she said, “if the wind agrees.”

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a brisk breeze. “It is only strength 2,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 2 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

Mara placed the ready pouch in Ada’s hands. “Keep it low and tied,” she said. Ada accepted it carefully. The pouch was no longer merely waiting at the post; it was now part of their working arrangement.

Ada placed the invitations in the pouch while Pip held its mouth open with careful claws. Together they tied it shut. The papers were secured inside, not merely imagined there. Pip whispered, “No heroic gusts.” Ada replied, “Only tested ones.”

Mara passed Ada the coil of twine. “A line gives the pouch a boundary,” she explained. Ada tested the cord between her fingers. “So Pip can guide the bundle without chasing it,” she replied.

Ada and Mara stretched the twine between safe roof posts and tied firm knots. Mara pulled the line once; it answered with a quiet twang. “That is a road with rails,” Ada said.

With the pouch tied to the guiding line, Ada watched the stopping point while Pip gave measured warm puffs. The pouch slid, paused, and slid again instead of flying. At the glasshouse, the invitations reached the labeled pots together. The labeled pots now held the complete invitation bundle, a bright row of proof that their careful arrangement had worked.

title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:
The invitations were ready, but the rooftops were not a simple road. Ada counted 4 papers, Pip warmed his cheeks for a helpful puff, and Mara checked the nearby pots. “No daring guesses,” Mara said. Ada nodded. “We will notice, test, and change our method if we need to.” Above them, the marker ribbon began to dance.

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a gentle breeze. “It is only strength 1,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Pip tried a tiny warm puff, but the ribbon bobbed sideways and nearly brushed a pot. He stopped at once. “My breath is wobbly today,” he admitted. Ada answered, “Then we will use your eyes and ears, not a big puff.”

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Ada peered along the roofline toward the glasshouse. The route was open, with no fallen tools or blocked stepping stones. She pointed it out to Mara. “That path may be useful,” she said, “if the wind agrees.”

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 1 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

Pip’s breath was not ready for cargo, so Ada and Mara chose the sheltered route. They carried small dry batches through the chimney nook, with Pip watching the ribbon and calling, “Gust coming!” Every invitation reached its safe resting place. The complete bundle now rested in the chimney nook, safely covered in its final arrangement beneath the shelter.

title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:
Before sunset, Ada had 4 garden-party invitations waiting at the roof post. Pip the young dragon stood beside her, eager to help, while Mara watched the roof paths and the planters below. The ribbon wind-marker flickered. “We need every invitation to arrive safely,” Ada said. “Then we should find out what the roof is telling us first.”

Pip gave the ribbon a tiny warm puff. It lifted neatly and settled without whipping away. His eyes widened. “I can make a small breeze,” he said. Ada grinned. “Small and steady is exactly what we need.”

Mara turned the cloth pouch inside out and found its loose seam. With twine and careful little stitches, she repaired it. She tugged the mouth twice. “Now it will hold,” she said, “but only because we checked it first.”

Ada peered along the roofline toward the glasshouse. The route was open, with no fallen tools or blocked stepping stones. She pointed it out to Mara. “That path may be useful,” she said, “if the wind agrees.”

They walked slowly past the planters and placed each paper with the labeled pots. “No flight needed,” Mara said. “Good noticing did the traveling.” The labeled pots now held the complete invitation bundle, a bright row of proof that their careful arrangement had worked.

title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:
The invitations were ready, but the rooftops were not a simple road. Ada counted 3 papers, Pip warmed his cheeks for a helpful puff, and Mara checked the nearby pots. “No daring guesses,” Mara said. Ada nodded. “We will notice, test, and change our method if we need to.” Above them, the marker ribbon began to dance.

Ada peered along the roofline toward the glasshouse. The route was open, with no fallen tools or blocked stepping stones. She pointed it out to Mara. “That path may be useful,” she said, “if the wind agrees.”

Pip tried a tiny warm puff, but the ribbon bobbed sideways and nearly brushed a pot. He stopped at once. “My breath is wobbly today,” he admitted. Ada answered, “Then we will use your eyes and ears, not a big puff.”

Mara turned the cloth pouch inside out and found its loose seam. With twine and careful little stitches, she repaired it. She tugged the mouth twice. “Now it will hold,” she said, “but only because we checked it first.”

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a brisk breeze. “It is only strength 2,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 2 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

Mara passed Ada the coil of twine. “A line gives the pouch a boundary,” she explained. Ada tested the cord between her fingers. “So Pip can guide the bundle without chasing it,” she replied.

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Pip’s breath was not ready for cargo, so Ada and Mara chose the sheltered route. They carried small dry batches through the chimney nook, with Pip watching the ribbon and calling, “Gust coming!” Every invitation reached its safe resting place. The complete bundle now rested in the chimney nook, safely covered in its final arrangement beneath the shelter.

title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:
The invitations were ready, but the rooftops were not a simple road. Ada counted 4 papers, Pip warmed his cheeks for a helpful puff, and Mara checked the nearby pots. “No daring guesses,” Mara said. Ada nodded. “We will notice, test, and change our method if we need to.” Above them, the marker ribbon began to dance.

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a gentle breeze. “It is only strength 1,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Ada peered along the roofline toward the glasshouse. The route was open, with no fallen tools or blocked stepping stones. She pointed it out to Mara. “That path may be useful,” she said, “if the wind agrees.”

Mara turned the cloth pouch inside out and found its loose seam. With twine and careful little stitches, she repaired it. She tugged the mouth twice. “Now it will hold,” she said, “but only because we checked it first.”

Pip gave the ribbon a tiny warm puff. It lifted neatly and settled without whipping away. His eyes widened. “I can make a small breeze,” he said. Ada grinned. “Small and steady is exactly what we need.”

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 1 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

The calm route was open, so Ada and Mara carried the dry invitations by hand. They walked slowly past the planters and placed each paper with the labeled pots. “No flight needed,” Mara said. “Good noticing did the traveling.” The labeled pots now held the complete invitation bundle, a bright row of proof that their careful arrangement had worked.

title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:
Before sunset, Ada had 4 garden-party invitations waiting at the roof post. Pip the young dragon stood beside her, eager to help, while Mara watched the roof paths and the planters below. The ribbon wind-marker flickered. “We need every invitation to arrive safely,” Ada said. “Then we should find out what the roof is telling us first.”

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Pip tried a tiny warm puff, but the ribbon bobbed sideways and nearly brushed a pot. He stopped at once. “My breath is wobbly today,” he admitted. Ada answered, “Then we will use your eyes and ears, not a big puff.”

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a brisk breeze. “It is only strength 2,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 2 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

Ada looked toward the glasshouse and found the route closed. A small gate barred the way. “That settles it,” she said. “We need the sheltered chimney nook instead of pretending a closed path is open.”

Mara placed the ready pouch in Ada’s hands. “Keep it low and tied,” she said. Ada accepted it carefully. The pouch was no longer merely waiting at the post; it was now part of their working arrangement.

Because the glasshouse route was closed, Mara lent Ada the light basket. “Cover the papers,” she warned. Ada nodded, and Pip peered over the rim. “A basket can travel on the safe side,” Ada said.

Mara passed Ada the coil of twine. “A line gives the pouch a boundary,” she explained. Ada tested the cord between her fingers. “So Pip can guide the bundle without chasing it,” she replied.

Ada and Mara stretched the twine between safe roof posts and tied firm knots. Mara pulled the line once; it answered with a quiet twang. “That is a road with rails,” Ada said.

Pip’s breath was not ready for cargo, so Ada and Mara chose the sheltered route. They carried small dry batches through the chimney nook, with Pip watching the ribbon and calling, “Gust coming!” Every invitation reached its safe resting place. The complete bundle now rested in the chimney nook, safely covered in its final arrangement beneath the shelter.

title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:
The invitations were ready, but the rooftops were not a simple road. Ada counted 3 papers, Pip warmed his cheeks for a helpful puff, and Mara checked the nearby pots. “No daring guesses,” Mara said. Ada nodded. “We will notice, test, and change our method if we need to.” Above them, the marker ribbon began to dance.

Ada peered along the roofline toward the glasshouse. The route was open, with no fallen tools or blocked stepping stones. She pointed it out to Mara. “That path may be useful,” she said, “if the wind agrees.”

Mara turned the cloth pouch inside out and found its loose seam. With twine and careful little stitches, she repaired it. She tugged the mouth twice. “Now it will hold,” she said, “but only because we checked it first.”

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a brisk breeze. “It is only strength 2,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Pip tried a tiny warm puff, but the ribbon bobbed sideways and nearly brushed a pot. He stopped at once. “My breath is wobbly today,” he admitted. Ada answered, “Then we will use your eyes and ears, not a big puff.”

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 2 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

Mara placed the ready pouch in Ada’s hands. “Keep it low and tied,” she said. Ada accepted it carefully. The pouch was no longer merely waiting at the post; it was now part of their working arrangement.

Mara passed Ada the coil of twine. “A line gives the pouch a boundary,” she explained. Ada tested the cord between her fingers. “So Pip can guide the bundle without chasing it,” she replied.

Pip’s breath was not ready for cargo, so Ada and Mara chose the sheltered route. They carried small dry batches through the chimney nook, with Pip watching the ribbon and calling, “Gust coming!” Every invitation reached its safe resting place. The complete bundle now rested in the chimney nook, safely covered in its final arrangement beneath the shelter.

title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:
Before sunset, Ada had 4 garden-party invitations waiting at the roof post. Pip the young dragon stood beside her, eager to help, while Mara watched the roof paths and the planters below. The ribbon wind-marker flickered. “We need every invitation to arrive safely,” Ada said. “Then we should find out what the roof is telling us first.”

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Mara turned the cloth pouch inside out and found its loose seam. With twine and careful little stitches, she repaired it. She tugged the mouth twice. “Now it will hold,” she said, “but only because we checked it first.”

Ada looked toward the glasshouse and found the route closed. A small gate barred the way. “That settles it,” she said. “We need the sheltered chimney nook instead of pretending a closed path is open.”

Pip gave the ribbon a tiny warm puff. It lifted neatly and settled without whipping away. His eyes widened. “I can make a small breeze,” he said. Ada grinned. “Small and steady is exactly what we need.”

Because the glasshouse route was closed, Mara lent Ada the light basket. “Cover the papers,” she warned. Ada nodded, and Pip peered over the rim. “A basket can travel on the safe side,” Ada said.

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a brisk breeze. “It is only strength 2,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 2 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

Mara placed the ready pouch in Ada’s hands. “Keep it low and tied,” she said. Ada accepted it carefully. The pouch was no longer merely waiting at the post; it was now part of their working arrangement.

Ada settled the invitations into the light basket. Pip helped lower the cloth cover, and Ada tucked every corner beneath the rim. The bundle could no longer skate away in a sudden breeze.

Mara passed Ada the coil of twine. “A line gives the pouch a boundary,” she explained. Ada tested the cord between her fingers. “So Pip can guide the bundle without chasing it,” she replied.

Ada and Mara stretched the twine between safe roof posts and tied firm knots. Mara pulled the line once; it answered with a quiet twang. “That is a road with rails,” Ada said.

Pip nudged the covered basket in short, gentle bursts. Ada watched its feet skim the safe route and called, “Stop!” whenever the basket neared an edge. It arrived in the chimney nook, where the invitations rested beneath shelter. The complete bundle now rested in the chimney nook, safely covered in its final arrangement beneath the shelter.

title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:
The invitations were ready, but the rooftops were not a simple road. Ada counted 3 papers, Pip warmed his cheeks for a helpful puff, and Mara checked the nearby pots. “No daring guesses,” Mara said. Ada nodded. “We will notice, test, and change our method if we need to.” Above them, the marker ribbon began to dance.

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a gentle breeze. “It is only strength 1,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 1 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

Ada peered along the roofline toward the glasshouse. The route was open, with no fallen tools or blocked stepping stones. She pointed it out to Mara. “That path may be useful,” she said, “if the wind agrees.”

Pip tried a tiny warm puff, but the ribbon bobbed sideways and nearly brushed a pot. He stopped at once. “My breath is wobbly today,” he admitted. Ada answered, “Then we will use your eyes and ears, not a big puff.”

Pip’s breath was not ready for cargo, so Ada and Mara chose the sheltered route. They carried small dry batches through the chimney nook, with Pip watching the ribbon and calling, “Gust coming!” Every invitation reached its safe resting place. The complete bundle now rested in the chimney nook, safely covered in its final arrangement beneath the shelter.

title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:
Before sunset, Ada had 3 garden-party invitations waiting at the roof post. Pip the young dragon stood beside her, eager to help, while Mara watched the roof paths and the planters below. The ribbon wind-marker flickered. “We need every invitation to arrive safely,” Ada said. “Then we should find out what the roof is telling us first.”

Pip tried a tiny warm puff, but the ribbon bobbed sideways and nearly brushed a pot. He stopped at once. “My breath is wobbly today,” he admitted. Ada answered, “Then we will use your eyes and ears, not a big puff.”

Ada peered along the roofline toward the glasshouse. The route was open, with no fallen tools or blocked stepping stones. She pointed it out to Mara. “That path may be useful,” she said, “if the wind agrees.”

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a gentle breeze. “It is only strength 1,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 1 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

The calm route was open, so Ada and Mara carried the dry invitations by hand. They walked slowly past the planters and placed each paper with the labeled pots. “No flight needed,” Mara said. “Good noticing did the traveling.” The labeled pots now held the complete invitation bundle, a bright row of proof that their careful arrangement had worked.

title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:
Before sunset, Ada had 3 garden-party invitations waiting at the roof post. Pip the young dragon stood beside her, eager to help, while Mara watched the roof paths and the planters below. The ribbon wind-marker flickered. “We need every invitation to arrive safely,” Ada said. “Then we should find out what the roof is telling us first.”

Ada peered along the roofline toward the glasshouse. The route was open, with no fallen tools or blocked stepping stones. She pointed it out to Mara. “That path may be useful,” she said, “if the wind agrees.”

Mara turned the cloth pouch inside out and found its loose seam. With twine and careful little stitches, she repaired it. She tugged the mouth twice. “Now it will hold,” she said, “but only because we checked it first.”

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a brisk breeze. “It is only strength 2,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 2 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

Mara placed the ready pouch in Ada’s hands. “Keep it low and tied,” she said. Ada accepted it carefully. The pouch was no longer merely waiting at the post; it was now part of their working arrangement.

Pip gave the ribbon a tiny warm puff. It lifted neatly and settled without whipping away. His eyes widened. “I can make a small breeze,” he said. Ada grinned. “Small and steady is exactly what we need.”

Mara passed Ada the coil of twine. “A line gives the pouch a boundary,” she explained. Ada tested the cord between her fingers. “So Pip can guide the bundle without chasing it,” she replied.

Ada and Mara stretched the twine between safe roof posts and tied firm knots. Mara pulled the line once; it answered with a quiet twang. “That is a road with rails,” Ada said.

Ada placed the invitations in the pouch while Pip held its mouth open with careful claws. Together they tied it shut. The papers were secured inside, not merely imagined there. Pip whispered, “No heroic gusts.” Ada replied, “Only tested ones.”

With the pouch tied to the guiding line, Ada watched the stopping point while Pip gave measured warm puffs. The pouch slid, paused, and slid again instead of flying. At the glasshouse, the invitations reached the labeled pots together. The labeled pots now held the complete invitation bundle, a bright row of proof that their careful arrangement had worked.

story:

Ada nodded. “We will notice, test, and change our method if we need to.” Above them, the marker ribbon began to dance.

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a gentle breeze. “It is only strength 1,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 1 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

Ada looked toward the glasshouse and found the route closed. A small gate barred the way. “That settles it,” she said. “We need the sheltered chimney nook instead of pretending a closed path is open.”

Because the glasshouse route was closed, Mara lent Ada the light basket. “Cover the papers,” she warned. Ada nodded, and Pip peered over the rim. “A basket can travel on the safe side,” Ada said.

Ada settled the invitations into the light basket. Pip helped lower the cloth cover, and Ada tucked every corner beneath the rim. The bundle could no longer skate away in a sudden breeze.

Pip gave the ribbon a tiny warm puff. It lifted neatly and settled without whipping away. His eyes widened. “I can make a small breeze,” he said. Ada grinned. “Small and steady is exactly what we need.”

Pip nudged the covered basket in short, gentle bursts. Ada watched its feet skim the safe route and called, “Stop!” whenever the basket neared an edge. It arrived in the chimney nook, where the invitations rested beneath shelter. The complete bundle now rested in the chimney nook, safely covered in its final arrangement beneath the shelter.

title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:
The invitations were ready, but the rooftops were not a simple road. Ada counted 3 papers, Pip warmed his cheeks for a helpful puff, and Mara checked the nearby pots. “No daring guesses,” Mara said. Ada nodded. “We will notice, test, and change our method if we need to.” Above them, the marker ribbon began to dance.

Pip tried a tiny warm puff, but the ribbon bobbed sideways and nearly brushed a pot. He stopped at once. “My breath is wobbly today,” he admitted. Ada answered, “Then we will use your eyes and ears, not a big puff.”

Ada peered along the roofline toward the glasshouse. The route was open, with no fallen tools or blocked stepping stones. She pointed it out to Mara. “That path may be useful,” she said, “if the wind agrees.”

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a brisk breeze. “It is only strength 2,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 2 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

Mara passed Ada the coil of twine. “A line gives the pouch a boundary,” she explained. Ada tested the cord between her fingers. “So Pip can guide the bundle without chasing it,” she replied.

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Ada and Mara stretched the twine between safe roof posts and tied firm knots. Mara pulled the line once; it answered with a quiet twang. “That is a road with rails,” Ada said.

Pip’s breath was not ready for cargo, so Ada and Mara chose the sheltered route. They carried small dry batches through the chimney nook, with Pip watching the ribbon and calling, “Gust coming!” Every invitation reached its safe resting place. The complete bundle now rested in the chimney nook, safely covered in its final arrangement beneath the shelter.

title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:
The invitations were ready, but the rooftops were not a simple road. Ada counted 4 papers, Pip warmed his cheeks for a helpful puff, and Mara checked the nearby pots. “No daring guesses,” Mara said. Ada nodded. “We will notice, test, and change our method if we need to.” Above them, the marker ribbon began to dance.

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a brisk breeze. “It is only strength 2,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Pip gave the ribbon a tiny warm puff. It lifted neatly and settled without whipping away. His eyes widened. “I can make a small breeze,” he said. Ada grinned. “Small and steady is exactly what we need.”

Ada looked toward the glasshouse and found the route closed. A small gate barred the way. “That settles it,” she said. “We need the sheltered chimney nook instead of pretending a closed path is open.”

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 2 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

Because the glasshouse route was closed, Mara lent Ada the light basket. “Cover the papers,” she warned. Ada nodded, and Pip peered over the rim. “A basket can travel on the safe side,” Ada said.

Ada settled the invitations into the light basket. Pip helped lower the cloth cover, and Ada tucked every corner beneath the rim. The bundle could no longer skate away in a sudden breeze.

Mara placed the ready pouch in Ada’s hands. “Keep it low and tied,” she said. Ada accepted it carefully. The pouch was no longer merely waiting at the post; it was now part of their working arrangement.

Mara passed Ada the coil of twine. “A line gives the pouch a boundary,” she explained. Ada tested the cord between her fingers. “So Pip can guide the bundle without chasing it,” she replied.

Pip nudged the covered basket in short, gentle bursts. Ada watched its feet skim the safe route and called, “Stop!” whenever the basket neared an edge. It arrived in the chimney nook, where the invitations rested beneath shelter. The complete bundle now rested in the chimney nook, safely covered in its final arrangement beneath the shelter.

title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:
Before sunset, Ada had 4 garden-party invitations waiting at the roof post. Pip the young dragon stood beside her, eager to help, while Mara watched the roof paths and the planters below. The ribbon wind-marker flickered. “We need every invitation to arrive safely,” Ada said. “Then we should find out what the roof is telling us first.”

Pip tried a tiny warm puff, but the ribbon bobbed sideways and nearly brushed a pot. He stopped at once. “My breath is wobbly today,” he admitted. Ada answered, “Then we will use your eyes and ears, not a big puff.”

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a brisk breeze. “It is only strength 2,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Ada peered along the roofline toward the glasshouse. The route was open, with no fallen tools or blocked stepping stones. She pointed it out to Mara. “That path may be useful,” she said, “if the wind agrees.”

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 2 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

Pip’s breath was not ready for cargo, so Ada and Mara chose the sheltered route. They carried small dry batches through the chimney nook, with Pip watching the ribbon and calling, “Gust coming!” Every invitation reached its safe resting place. The complete bundle now rested in the chimney nook, safely covered in its final arrangement beneath the shelter.

title: Invitations Above the Roofs
story:
The invitations were ready, but the rooftops were not a simple road. Ada counted 3 papers, Pip warmed his cheeks for a helpful puff, and Mara checked the nearby pots. “No daring guesses,” Mara said. Ada nodded. “We will notice, test, and change our method if we need to.” Above them, the marker ribbon began to dance.

Ada lifted the top invitation by its corner and checked the stack. The paper was dry and un-torn. She smoothed one curled edge. “Good,” she said. “We can carry these, but we must keep them from fluttering loose.”

Pip gave the ribbon a tiny warm puff. It lifted neatly and settled without whipping away. His eyes widened. “I can make a small breeze,” he said. Ada grinned. “Small and steady is exactly what we need.”

Ada looked toward the glasshouse and found the route closed. A small gate barred the way. “That settles it,” she said. “We need the sheltered chimney nook instead of pretending a closed path is open.”

Ada leaned close to the ribbon without grabbing it. It streamed toward the chimney, then relaxed. She watched twice before deciding the wind was a gentle breeze. “It is only strength 1,” she told herself, “but that is enough to matter.”

Because the glasshouse route was closed, Mara lent Ada the light basket. “Cover the papers,” she warned. Ada nodded, and Pip peered over the rim. “A basket can travel on the safe side,” Ada said.

Ada explained what she had seen: the ribbon showed strength 1 wind. Mara listened rather than glancing at the sky. “Thank you,” she said. “Now I can lend the carrier that fits the weather.”

Ada settled the invitations into the light basket. Pip helped lower the cloth cover, and Ada tucked every corner beneath the rim. The bundle could no longer skate away in a sudden breeze.

Pip nudged the covered basket in short, gentle bursts. Ada watched its feet skim the safe route and called, “Stop!” whenever the basket neared an edge. It arrived in the chimney nook, where the invitations rested beneath shelter. The complete bundle now rested in the chimney nook, safely covered in its final arrangement beneath the shelter.
